Set Order of Age Group Levels for a Reporting Tree

Source: R/age_set_order_tree.R
age_set_order_tree.Rd

Modify the levels attribute of labels so that age groups are ordered as a reporting tree: the most detailed age groups first, then broader age groups, then age not stated.

Usage

age_set_order_tree(
  labels,
  interpret_fail = c("error", "warn", "silent"),
  x_arg = rlang::caller_arg(labels),
  call = rlang::current_env()
)

Arguments

labels

Vector of age group labels.

interpret_fail

Action if element of labels cannot be interpreted. Choices are "error" (the default), "warn", and "silent".

x_arg

Name of labels to use in error and warning messages. Defaults to the expression supplied for labels. A function that calls this function can supply its own name, such as "data$age".

call

Execution environment of the function to name in error and warning messages. The default is this function itself. A function that calls this function can supply call = rlang::current_env(), so that messages name it instead.

Value

Factor with the same length as labels.

Details

In a reporting tree, age groups nest: any two age groups either do not overlap, or one contains the other. Reporting trees arise, for instance, in census tables where most records have detailed ages ("0-4", "5-9", ...), some have only broad ages ("0-14", "15+"), and some have no age at all ("Missing").

Levels are ordered as follows:

  1. Leaves, that is, age groups that contain no other age group, ordered by lower limit.

  2. Broader age groups, ordered so that each age group comes after all age groups inside it, and before any age group entirely above it. For instance, "15-64", "65+", and "15+" are ordered "15-64", "65+", "15+".

  3. Labels that could not be interpreted, if interpret_fail is "warn" or "silent".

  4. Labels for missing values, as defined by age_is_missing().

Different labels that describe the same age group, such as "0-4" and "Under 5", are placed next to each other, in the order in which they first appear.

Leaves do not need to lie at the same depth in the tree. For instance, a tree can have a broad group "65+" and no broad groups at younger ages, so that "0-4" sits directly below the root while "70-74" sits below "65+".

age_set_order_tree() checks only that the age groups nest. It does not check, for instance, that the leaves cover all ages. Labels for totals, as defined by age_is_total(), are not part of a reporting tree, and cause an error. Some tables use "Total" to mean age not stated. In such cases, recode the total to "Missing" before calling age_set_order_tree(), for instance using age[age_is_total(age)] <- "Missing".

If labels is not a factor, and so does not have levels, it is converted to a factor before the ordering is performed. age_set_order_tree() has no effect on the values of labels. Only the levels are changed.

See also

  • age_set_order() Order age groups by lower limit

  • age_is_missing() Identify labels for missing values

  • period_set_order_tree() Period equivalent of age_set_order_tree()

  • cohort_set_order_tree() Cohort equivalent of age_set_order_tree()

Examples

labels <- c("Missing", "15+", "0-14", "70+", "60-69", "50-59",
            "40-49", "30-39", "20-29", "15-19", "10-14", "5-9", "0-4")
age_set_order_tree(labels)
#>  [1] Missing 15+     0-14    70+     60-69   50-59   40-49   30-39   20-29  
#> [10] 15-19   10-14   5-9     0-4    
#> 13 Levels: 0-4 5-9 10-14 15-19 20-29 30-39 40-49 50-59 60-69 70+ 0-14 ... Missing

## three levels, with leaves at different depths
labels <- c(age_labels_five(lower_last = 85),
            "0-14", "15+", "15-64", "65+", "Missing")
levels(age_set_order_tree(labels))
#>  [1] "0-4"     "5-9"     "10-14"   "15-19"   "20-24"   "25-29"   "30-34"  
#>  [8] "35-39"   "40-44"   "45-49"   "50-54"   "55-59"   "60-64"   "65-69"  
#> [15] "70-74"   "75-79"   "80-84"   "85+"     "0-14"    "15-64"   "65+"    
#> [22] "15+"     "Missing"
